en: An Elucidation of the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* (Ba Shi Gui Ju):
Composed by Zhenke, Explaining the First Five Consciousnesses.

"Nature-objects, direct perception, and the three natures apply to all"—this statement refers to the first five consciousnesses. Among the three types of objects, they perceive only nature-objects; among the three types of valid cognition, they are exclusively direct perception;
and among the three natures, they apply to all three.

"Nature-object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) refers to the various objective forms that are perceived without being associated with names or conventions, thereby apprehending the object's own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to blue, yellow, red, and white; "name" (*nāman*) refers to the designations of long, short, square, and round.

"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to the immediate and clear cognition of an object, free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The nature-object belongs to the objective realm, while direct perception belongs to the mind. [These] are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
These are the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral natures. All three natures are universally applicable because the nature of the five consciousnesses is not constant or uniform.

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*), if one asserts that it is constituted by eight factors—the sense organs and their objects as subject and object—this falls into the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Thus, there is no such objective realm; yet this realm manifests before one, like an image reflected in a clear mirror, serene and vividly apparent, without the arising of discrimination.
This is what is called the "true realm. Although the two natures of good and evil exist within the five consciousnesses, they remain without discrimination.
Because illumination arises from this, it is pervasive.
The three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two levels and are divided into nine stages within the three realms.
From the hells up to the six heavens of the desire realm, all constitute the single Desire Realm.

The realms: the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) consists of the four dhyānas and has four stages; the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of the four *ākāśas* and has four stages. Together, these constitute the nine stages.
The Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called the "Stage of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies" (*pañcagatimiśravāsabhūmi*); all five consciousnesses are present there.

The First Dhyāna Heaven is called the "Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukhabhūmi*); this constitutes the second stage. Therein, only the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body exist; the nose and tongue [consciousnesses] are absent.
Regarding the two consciousnesses: because there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), from the third dhyāna level upward, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are entirely absent.

The two lines—"the universal (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), the two intermediate, the eight great [afflictions], and greed, anger, and delusion"—refer to the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the five sensory consciousnesses. There are five universal factors, five object-specific factors, and the wholesome mental factors.
Eleven: two secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), eight major secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*), and six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
Now, there remain only the three—greed, hatred, and delusion. Together with the thirty-four mental factors (*caitta*), these are all spontaneous and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
The five consciousnesses share a common basis in the pure material sense organs (*śubha-rūpa-indriya*).
Here, "pure material" refers to the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*), which can only be perceived by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

That which falls within the realm of physical form is the ephemeral sense organ (*vṛtti-indriya*); how could this possibly illuminate objects? It is because the ultimate sense organ exists that the consciousnesses are able to perceive their respective objects.
It is said that the five consciousnesses arise based on the same dominant sense faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding the phrase "nine conditions for seven and eight, with favorable proximity":
the nine conditions are space, light, the faculty, the object, attention (*manasikāra*), discrimination, the defiled basis, the pure basis, and the fundamental basis, which is the seed.
My son, visual consciousness arises endowed with nine conditions; auditory consciousness proceeds from only eight, because it excludes the condition of light;
olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses have only seven, because they exclude both the conditions of space and light.

The "three combined" and "two separated" refer to the observation that the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through contact (*saṃyukta*), whereas the two consciousnesses of eye and ear apprehend their objects without contact (*viprayukta*). "Observation" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) which is the subjective perceiver;
"objects of the world" refers to the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) which is the objective perceived.
"The fool finds it difficult to distinguish between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the faculties (*indriya*).

This refers to the foolish *śrāvakas* of the Hīnayāna who do not understand that both the faculties and consciousness each possess seeds and manifest activity (*samudācāra*), and thus assume that the faculties and consciousness arise from one another.
They fail to realize that while the seeds and manifest activity of the faculties can only direct consciousness, [consciousness does not likewise direct the faculties].
Regarding seeds and manifestations: if the sense faculties serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness, then they may be said to "produce" consciousness;

however, one cannot say so from the perspective of consciousness itself, because consciousness possesses its own generative seeds. Since the followers of the Hīnayāna have not yet destroyed the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa), they lack full understanding of phenomena and thus find it difficult to distinguish [between these two].

The contemplation of emptiness through the transformation-aspect (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is exclusively the subsequently-attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); even within the state of fruition (*phala*), it still does not directly designate the ultimate truth.

The Buddha possesses both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently-attained wisdom. Fundamental wisdom is the wisdom of reality (*bhūtārtha-jñāna*); it can directly take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.

Subsequently-attained wisdom is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*); it can only comprehend the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), but cannot directly take True Suchness as its object. This refers to the stage of fruition.

The Buddha has already destroyed the delusions of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and is able to employ his six sense faculties interchangeably (*ṣaḍ-indriya-eka-vṛtti*). He transforms and gives rise to objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), yet further contemplates the emptiness of these objects.

Because he does not recognize the first five consciousnesses as well as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, he mistakenly identifies [his realization] as subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

He does not realize that subsequently attained wisdom is derived from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Although the Lesser Vehicle possesses [the wisdoms of] suchness (*yathābhūta*) and measure (*yathāmātra*), [it lacks this realization].
The two wisdoms differ only in name; how could they truly be the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*)?

Even within the state of Buddhahood, the subsequently attained wisdom does not fully express the ultimate reality (*tathatā*); how much less so while on the path of causes? "Expressing" means to accord with or penetrate.

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), and therefore it directly perceives *tathatā*. Subsequently attained wisdom arises from the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and is thus conceptual (*savikalpa*). Therefore...
They are unable to directly perceive the principle of non-conceptuality.

In the Hīnayāna, non-self is taken as *tathatā* (suchness). By severing the conceptual attachments of the six consciousnesses, one is able to employ the six sense organs interchangeably, which they consider to be the direct perception of *tathatā*.
The verse says: The Buddhas of the Small Vehicle and the Fruit-Head [Sravakas] possess only names in theory and logic; they are deluded by names and do not know their true meaning.
Doubting the Great [Vehicle], they give rise to contention. The five consciousnesses share a single awakening; thus, the eye could hear and the ear see.

This is truly not the fault of the original faculties, but the fault lies with the one who discriminates. Therefore, when seeing and thinking are destroyed, the six faculties immediately function interchangeably.
That minor [teacher] did not know this; he had not yet investigated the seven, eight, and five. When the three [truths] became clear to him, his arbitrary calculations naturally collapsed.
Having collapsed them, he abandoned his former doctrines and returned to the Mahāyāna with sorrow. Kumārajīva was his first teacher;
suspecting that Kumārajīva also possessed such discernment, once he realized the Great Principle, he again took Kumārajīva as his teacher.
The Perfectly Luminous first arises, achieving the untainted (*anāsrava*); the three types of transformation-bodies cease the wheel of suffering.

The five sense-consciousnesses follow the eighth consciousness; within the state of Buddhahood, the eighth consciousness is transformed into the untainted pure consciousness (*vimala-vijñāna*), and its associated mental factors (*caitta*) become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). As it suddenly manifests before one, it is called "the first."

When [the transformation] arises, the first five consciousnesses immediately become untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the three types of bodies: the "Transformation Body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) is one of the three bodies—Dharma, Enjoyment, and Transformation.
The "Great Transformation Body" measuring one thousand *zhang* is for Bodhisattvas in the four stages of application (*prayoga*) of the Mahāyāna.

The "Small Transformation Body" measuring sixteen *zhang* is for Bodhisattvas in the three stages of accumulation (*saṃbhāra*) of the Mahāyāna, as well as for those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), appearing in accordance with their respective types.

The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) universally covers the three vehicles and equally benefits those in the six realms of existence, thereby bringing rest to the wheel of suffering of sentient beings.
The first eight lines clarify the out-flowing (sāsrava) [dharmas], while the latter four lines clarify the non-out-flowing (anāsrava) [dharmas].
The sixth consciousness is accompanied by [mental factors] whose capacity for performing wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate actions is not fixed.
It operates through the three natures, the three types of valid cognition, and the three objects; its cycling through the three realms is easily understood.

The three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the three means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and non-cognition; and the three types of objects—natures-only images, reflected images, and substantial images—are all mutually pervasive.
"Inference" (比) refers to knowing through analogy. "Non-cognition" (非) refers to that which exists conventionally but lacks ultimate reality; it is an inference that fails to reach its mark.
There are two types of objects with a substantial basis (*sadravyālambana*). When the mind takes the mind as its object, the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* arises from both ends;

because it arises carrying the actual substantial basis, it is called "true *sadravya*. When the mind takes form (*rūpa*) as its object, the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* arises solely from one end, the *darśana-bhāga*;
because it arises as a transformation carrying [the basis], it is called "semblance *sadravya*. There are also two types of solitary images (*kevala-chāyā*); the first is...
Substantial, solitary images: the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs all arise by depending on a substance. There is one type that is a solitary image without a substance:

the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed from conditions such as empty flowers, rabbit horns, and the past or future. These are shadows of the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that have already fallen away;
they depend solely on the past five objects and the shadows of the five objects transformed from the future, but do not depend on the five objects currently present.
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses of a previous life grasped the shadows of dharmas to form the seeds of the physical form in this life;

now, in this life, one again gives rise to shadows based on that form, which are the seeds for receiving a physical form in a future life. If one can now apply contemplation with the six consciousnesses to shatter [these seeds],...
When one realizes the nature of self-grasping and does not grasp at mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), one will no longer receive a body of segmented birth.
The cycling of the six consciousnesses through the three realms is manifest and easy to understand;
however, the fifty-one associated mental factors (*caitta*) are subtle and difficult to perceive.

This phrase indicates the number [of categories]. The two phrases "nature" (*prakṛti*) and "realm" (*dhātu*) establish the names. It is intended that sentient beings, by means of the names, shall elucidate the meanings;

by means of the meanings, they shall realize the principles; by realizing the principles, they shall achieve their application; and achieving their application consists in the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
As stated above, achieving the application serves to embody the Way (*tattva*); embodying the Way serves to establish virtue (*guṇa*).
Good and evil are assigned according to the circumstances of the moment.

When the six consciousnesses encounter a wholesome object, they are associated with wholesome mental factors; when they encounter unwholesome or neutral objects, [they are associated with their respective factors].
Because it is associated with unwholesome and neutral mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*), it is said to be "individually assigned. This is merely an ordinary condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), even when a wholesome mind is vigorous and accompanied by unwholesome mental factors, it becomes wholesome.
The three natures, the three realms,
and the five feelings are constantly shifting and transforming; the six consciousnesses, together with the five feelings of sorrow, joy, suffering, pleasure, and equanimity,
are perpetually undergoing change and transformation.
The root afflictions, such as faith and the rest,

are connected with the six root afflictions, the twenty secondary afflictions, the eleven wholesome factors, and so forth; furthermore, the five universal [mental factors], the five object-specific ones,
and the four indeterminate ones— these fifty-one in total— are likewise connected by their nature, realm, feeling-tone, and other shifting characteristics.
When moving the body or uttering speech, it alone is the most preeminent;
at the time of moving the body or uttering speech, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is the most excellent among the eight consciousnesses, because it is that which possesses sentient beings (*sattva*).
"Projection and fulfillment" refers to the power of karma that projects and brings about [rebirth];
"fulfillment" means making complete. It is said that the six consciousnesses are able to create karma and summon its fruit, initiating the stage of the Joyous Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Because the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) severs the conceptualization of self and dharmas,
this consciousness is transformed into the untainted (*anāsrava*) at the first moment of mind in the First Ground; this is because it has severed the two types of dualistic grasping—
conceptualizing self and dharmas.
The innate [afflictions], namely the non-conceptual dual grasping at self and phenomena—
both active obsessions and latent propensities— are co-nascent with birth; at this stage they have not yet been severed,
remaining as entanglements and dormant latencies because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have not been abandoned.
After the Ground of Far-Going, it is purely untainted; its observation is perfectly luminous, illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
The Ground of Far-Going is the seventh ground. Prior to this ground, tainted and untainted states arise in alternation.
Upon reaching this ground, however, the two obstacles that arise spontaneously never again manifest, and the mind is associated exclusively with the purely untainted.
The object-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) also transforms into the wisdom of wondrous observation, brilliantly and perfectly illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
The seventh consciousness,
possessing both substantiality and concealment, pervades both the phenomenal and the fundamental.

Regarding the seven consciousnesses among the three types of objects, they take the "object with substance" (*sadravyālambana*) as their objective support. Among the three moral natures, they possess only the nature of being obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
"Obscured" means that it veils the true nature; because it pervades the six functioning consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it refers to the fundamental eighth consciousness.
Because it pervades both the functioning and the fundamental [consciousnesses], it is said that the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) arises at both ends.

The seventh consciousness takes the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its internal self. The seventh consciousness is the mind, and the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is also the mind;

therefore it is said that "the mind taking the mind as an object is truly a 'concrete object' (*sadravya-svabhāva*)," because the eighth consciousness constitutes its objective essence (*ālambana-prakṛti*).
Since the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-portion of the eighth consciousness as its internal self, the seeing-portion of the eighth consciousness is itself the seventh consciousness.
The primary position: when the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses takes form as its object, this is precisely the seventh consciousness taking form as its object.

Because form is not real, it is said to be "apparently with a mediated essence" (*sādṛśya-satpratibimba*). Question: A "mediated essence" means that one brings forth a clear perception by mediating upon the original essence (*bimba*) of the eighth consciousness; how then does this apply to the seventh consciousness?

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): the eight consciousnesses are able to store all things; that which is stored includes the entire body, the sensory faculties, and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*).

Because they are grasped as a self through the attachment of craving for "I," the eight consciousnesses thus possess an objective realm. From where does this realm arise? It arises from the six consciousnesses.

Thus, one knows that the seventh consciousness originally has no independent substance or position; its *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is produced from the two heads—the sixth and the eighth consciousnesses.
Regarding the phrase "grasping at a self according to conditions":
this consciousness, in its non-conceptual grasping at both self and phenomena, operates spontaneously and continuously; therefore, it is said to "grasp at a self according to conditions."
The eight universal [mental factors] are associated with the five object-specific ones, wisdom (*prajñā*), greed, delusion, self-view, and pride;
the great ground [factors] consist of only these eight. The universal factors are five; the object-specific factors are limited to wisdom. Among the root afflictions, only four are present.
Greed, delusion, views, and pride are such [mental factors].

The notion of a self (*ātman*) that constantly and critically deliberates does not accompany the first five consciousnesses, as they are neither constant nor critical. The six consciousnesses are critical but not constant; only this consciousness (the *ālaya-vijñāna*) is both constant and critical.
Through speculative reasoning and measurement, one clings to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses as the self; hence it is said that the mark of selfhood follows.
Sentient beings are perpetually mired in confusion day and night, for the four afflictions and the eight major [secondary] afflictions arise in conjunction.
Since one clings to the eight consciousnesses as the internal self, sentient beings remain constantly within the long night of birth and death. And so on...
Self-awareness (manas) is associated with the four afflictions and the eight great [afflictions], and thus gives rise to the four afflictions; these are the four root afflictions.
The sixth consciousness is called the basis of defilement and purity.

All eight consciousnesses are equally *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses). However, when only the six consciousnesses engage in contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), all the consciousnesses evolve together;

thus, the term "evolving" (*pravṛtti*) is applied specifically to the six consciousnesses. The seventh consciousness is termed the "basis of defilement and purity" (*kliṣṭa-śuddhi-āśraya*), because the six consciousnesses possess conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

The seven consciousnesses are without discrimination; that which possesses discrimination arises based on that which is without discrimination. Because it is without discrimination, it is close to the insentient.
"The nature of equality in the initial moment of supreme joy— I constantly crush the effortless conduct [of those who cling to it]."
In every stage (*bhūmi*), there are fully present the three moments of mind—initial, middle, and final—which correspond respectively to entering, abiding, and emerging.

At the initial moment of the first stage, this consciousness severs one portion of ignorance and is thereby transformed into what is called "incomplete" [mirror-like wisdom], which resembles the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
This is because it functions within the causal stage. Effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) is the non-conceptual state of the eighth bhūmi;
since the two types of grasping—toward self and phenomena—are completely severed at this point, it is said that "I am ever crushing," which constitutes the true wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
When the six consciousnesses reach the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), they transform into the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation).

How then is it that the seventh consciousness transforms into the *samatā-jñāna* (the wisdom of equality) at the initial moment of the first stage? It is because once the six consciousnesses have reached the completion of contemplation, they transform into the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*;
whereas at the time one first initiates contemplation, [the seventh consciousness] transforms into what resembles the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*.
The Tathāgata manifests the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) for the sake of those who are the objects of his influence—the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Within the state of Buddhahood, he manifests ten kinds of bodies of enjoyment for others; these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are precisely the objects of his influence.
The nature of the eighth consciousness is exclusively non-obscured;
its five universal mental factors are its causes within this consciousness. Among the three natures, it is exclusively of the non-obscured indeterminate nature. When perceiving objects, its aspect—
Its associated mental factors consist solely of the five omnipresent (sarvatraga) factors.

Regarding its realm and stage, this consciousness arises within the three realms and nine stages in accordance with the karmic power of others; it arises in accordance with the wholesome or unwholesome karmic power of the six consciousnesses. Because...

Because the eight consciousnesses are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand them; due to their deluded attachments, they are able to engage in disputes with the Master regarding this consciousness, which is most subtle.
Therefore, the Śrāvakas who follow the foolish teachings do not believe that this exists, relying only on—

The first six consciousnesses receive perfuming and maintain seeds; they sever and exhaust the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), yet they cling to this as the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

They cling to the mutual functioning of the six sense organs as the wisdom of phenomena (*yāvadbhāva-jñāna*). Because ignorance has not been fully destroyed, the masters of the Mahāyāna treatises [have said this].
Through repeated debate and analysis, it is proven that this consciousness exists.

Vast and inexhaustible as the Three Piṭakas, it is called the "capable store" (ālaya) because it maintains the seeds without loss; it is called the "stored-in" (āśraya) because it receives the perfuming of both defiled and pure factors. The seven consciousnesses...

It is called "appropriating" (*ālaya*) because it is grasped as a self. Because the essence and function of the three *ālayas* are profound and vast, ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle do not comprehend them.
The seven waves are the objects, and the eighth consciousness is like a clear, tranquil abyss. Due to the first seven consciousnesses, which grasp external objects as winds, [the waves] arise.
It has "waves" as its ears.
It receives perfuming and maintains seeds within the root-body and the vessel-world;
this consciousness is able to receive the prior perfuming of defilement and purity, and is able to maintain the seeds of the root-body and the vessel-world. The "roots" are the six [sense organs].
The faculties are the internal world; the physical body is the vessel of the external world.
Departing last and arriving first as the presiding lord, it is this consciousness alone that serves as the sovereign of the collective retribution.
"Before the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one merely abandons the storehouse; after the Vajra Path, the maturation is empty. The eighth ground is the Immovable Ground.
When this consciousness first reaches this ground, it merely abandons the "capable storehouse," the "storehouse that is stored," and the "clinging storehouse.

Upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) after the Vajra Path, [the maturation ceases]. As for "maturation" (*vipāka*): it is that which matures through transformation. It is "different" (*vi-*) because...

They ripen at different times; they ripen as different types [of existence]. Only after the path of the vajra does one sever the ignorance of the sign of arising (*utpatti-nimitta-avidyā*), and only then do the seeds of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*) become empty.
"Vajra-contemplation wisdom" (*vajra-vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is the name for this wisdom; it is so called because of its hardness and sharpness, being able to destroy all ignorance. There is...
Regarding birth, abiding, change, and cessation: when the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) is empty, the single momentary flash of ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise empty.
The Great Perfect Sphere, free from defilement, simultaneously manifests and universally illumines the dust-like lands of the ten directions.
When this consciousness reaches the stage of Buddhahood, it is transformed into the supreme, untainted pure essence, designated as the "Stainless Consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*).
Simultaneously with its arising, it accords with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and universally illumines the perfectly luminous worlds of the ten directions.
*Commentary on the Brief Explanation of Consciousness-Only*:
Now, to probe the mysteries of yin and yang, to encompass the essence of transformation and creation, to penetrate the source of the vast chaos, and to shatter the primordial miasma...
The Cavern of Chaos transcends Confucianism and Daoism in its singular loftiness; it stands preeminent among the hundred schools, profound and vast.

It has never happened that one could seek elsewhere than the school of *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only). For it negates the existence of external objects while distinguishing consciousness from the void. By negating objects, there is nothing existing outside of consciousness;
by distinguishing [consciousness] from the void, it is not the same as a barren extinction. Thus, it levels the pits of eternalism and nihilism and blocks the path of arising and ceasing.

This path clearly manifests the Middle Way and establishes the definitive principles of Hetuvidyā (Logic). It is beyond the reach of Māras and heretics, and is followed alike by both ordinary beings and sages.
Now, as for consciousness, there are eight kinds, distinguished between the mind-king (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).

Were it not for a wisdom that is empty and luminous, with a power of discernment so wondrous and transcendent, how could one easily peer into its inner precincts? Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the others, I have roughly investigated the origins from which they arise. Directly...
By means of True Suchness (tathatā), illumination reaches its limit and turns back into obscurity; thus, the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing are conjoined.
This is called the "self-attesting portion" (svasaṃvittibhāga). It is like a person who has suddenly fallen into a stupor: although they hear the voices of others, they cannot discern them clearly.

Can one call this state "awake"? Yet, because they cannot discern clearly, can one call it "stuporous"? That one hears the voices of others while in this state is what is meant by being "half-asleep and half-awake."

These two aspects are intertwined; they are the very gateway between delusion and awakening. During such moments, if someone calls out to one, the darkness follows the awakening; if no one calls, the awakening follows the darkness.
Once awakening follows darkness, one is unable to discern external objects and does not even dream, remaining merely in a state of profound obscurity.
This is called the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (the self-verifying aspect). In these moments, there is no distinction between subject and object; it is a state of dark, undifferentiated stillness.
Yet it alone remains. After a short while, one suddenly dreams of various forms of sorrow and joy, suffering and pleasure.

From the perspective of that which is capable of observing, this is called the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga); that which is the object of observation is the "image-part" (nimitta-bhāga). Someone may ask:
"Do these two parts, the seeing and the image, arise sequentially, or do they arise simultaneously? I respond to him: "As for the claim that the seeing and image parts arise sequentially..."
Within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), non-conceptualization is not admitted; as soon as conceptualization arises, direct perception ceases.

This is called "antagonistic arising," wherein the subject and object are no longer identical. Since these four divisions are the very foundation of the eight consciousnesses, those who are intent upon this school must not fail to be attentive to them.
If the four divisions are thoroughly penetrated, then the framework of the eight consciousnesses will be understood. Reflect deeply on this.
This is half [of the explanation].

Now, the eight consciousnesses and four divisions constitute the fundamental framework of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school. The *ālaya-vijñāna*, the *manas-vijñāna*, the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminating consciousness), and the five consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—these are called the eight consciousnesses.
The *sākṣāt-svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (the division of self-witnessing of the witness) and the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (the division of self-witnessing).

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*)—these are called the four parts. To speak of their ultimate source, the eight consciousnesses and their four parts originally possess no distinct substance;
they arise as various phenomena solely through *tathatā* (suchness) responding to conditions. Now, the principle of *tathatā* responding to conditions is most difficult to comprehend.
This is because *tathatā* is pure and fundamentally free from any taint; how, then, could it suddenly give rise to responding to conditions? Regarding this—

If one continues this investigation without ceasing, one will suddenly awaken and enter [realization]. Regarding what are called the eight consciousnesses and four divisions, there will be no need for even a slight examination;
one will then be able to understand the texts on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) with perfect clarity. Therefore it is said:

"If one penetrates the School of Nature (*xingzong*) but does not penetrate the School of Characteristics (*xiangzong*), then what is seen by the School of Nature is still not yet complete. If one penetrates the School of Characteristics but does not penetrate the School of Nature, then what is seen by the School of Characteristics..."
Furthermore, one may have attained mastery over both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*), yet fail to awaken to the Chan of Bodhidharma;
this is like the "Dragon of Duke Ye," whose head and horns appear perfectly complete when viewed from afar, yet cannot bring forth rain or thunder to end a severe drought.
Therefore, those who aspire to transcend the world and shoulder the burden of the Dharma must cultivate not only nature, characteristics, and Chan, but also... [the rest of the path].
I, your humble servant, dare not fail to exhaust my sincerity and devote my attention to this.

However, as the names and meanings within the *Yogācāra* (Consciousness-Only) school are numerous, they are truly not easy to clarify unless one possesses a subtle and profound intellect and conducts a meticulous, thorough investigation. For now, I shall provide a general outline, offering a brief discussion and commentary;

this will merely serve to give a rough understanding to the ignorant and young. Generally speaking, the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) extends to the preceding [consciousnesses] of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five consciousnesses should be treated together for exposition; they seem easier to clarify.

This is because both the ālayavijñāna and the first five consciousnesses belong to direct perception (pratyakṣa), and both are transformations within the superior grade of fruition. As for the seventh and sixth consciousnesses...

Thus, all three grades are complete. As for these three grades: the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) constitutes the lower grade; the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) constitutes the middle grade;
and the Ultimate Path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*) constitutes the upper grade. Therefore, [the transformation] occurs within the seven or six causal factors. Someone may ask:

"If the first five consciousnesses achieve the category of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) associated mental states to benefit sentient beings in their present bodies, why was it stated previously that the eighth [consciousness] achieves the uncontaminated? This is because, at the initial stage of perfect illumination...
"Arising" refers to the mental complex associated with the eighth consciousness, as it constitutes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Consequently, the first five sense organs are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) manifested by the eighth consciousness; since the fundamental consciousness that manifests them has already become untainted (*anāsrava*), the five sense organs it manifests must likewise naturally become untainted.
Once the five sense organs that give rise to cognition have become untainted, the five consciousnesses that they give rise to consequently [become untainted].

How could there be any doubt that they become untainted (*anāsrava*)? Someone asks: "If it is said that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), why then do you speak instead of 'associated mental factors' (*samprayukta-caitta*)?
The response is: The tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "These four categories encompass all conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) of the Buddha-stage without exception.
This refers to the transformation of the characteristics of the tainted (*sāsrava*) eighth, seventh, sixth, and fifth consciousnesses.

In the *Cittotpāda-parivarta*, it is stated that wisdom (*jñāna*) is attained in accordance with the sequence [of the stages]. Although it is not consciousness (*vijñāna*), it relies upon consciousness; because the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is primary, it is said that "consciousness transforms to attain [wisdom].
Furthermore, in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*), wisdom is weak and consciousness is strong, whereas in the state free from outflows (*anāsrava*), wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak.

To encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness, it is therefore said that "consciousness transforms into wisdom. This is the meaning of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) according to the Mahāyāna.

It is said: "To say that [an object] 'bears its own characteristics' (dai-ji-sō) means that there are two distinct meanings for both 'bearing' (dai) and 'own characteristics' (ji-sō). Regarding the two meanings of 'bearing':
first is 'clinging-bearing' (kyō-dai), which refers to the cognizing mind directly grasping the essence of the object while cognizing it;

second is 'transformation-bearing' (hen-dai), which refers to the cognizing mind transforming and giving rise to a representational aspect (sō-bun) while cognizing it. That which is directly grasped is called the 'real object' (jitsu-kyō); that which is transformed and given rise to..."
This is called the "provisional object. What is a provisional object? It is the reflection of the real object. What is this reflection? It refers to the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
These directly grasp the real object and perceive it spontaneously, without being accompanied by names or concepts; they function within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It is like a clear mirror that reflects whatever object is placed before it; originally, it has no intentionality. As soon as one perceives beauty or ugliness, the direct perception has already ceased. This is precisely...

This falls into the category of *anumāna* (inference). I understand that these are merely shadows of provisional objects, which are the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, the cognizing mind transforms and gives rise to its own *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) as an object;

this too is a provisional object. Now, within the school of Sthiramati, it is falsely claimed that the five untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses can cognize *tathatā* (suchness) while still in the causal stage.
Little do they realize that for the five consciousnesses to become wisdom (*jñāna*), they must necessarily depend upon the transformation of the eighth consciousness.
It is [only] after [attaining] fundamental wisdom that the five consciousnesses are transformed into the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Why is this wisdom referred to here as "subsequently attained" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)? It is because it is attained subsequent to the fundamental [wisdom]. This refers to the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness.

This is because they all belong to the same transformation within the fruit of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). They claim that within the cause, the five consciousnesses have not yet transformed into wisdom, yet they are able to take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object;
how could this not be non-delusory? Even if, upon reaching the fruit, the consciousnesses have indeed transformed into wisdom, they are only able to illuminate the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

Yet they are unable to take True Suchness (tathatā) as their object. Therefore, Master Hufa said: "If even within the fruit [of enlightenment] it does not yet fully express the Truth, how much less so within the cause?
*Explanation of the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses* (concludes).
